about.title: La Habra Heights Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: La Habra Heights is a small, hillside community, but its residents still commute to jobs in construction, landscaping, delivery, agriculture, and small-business trades across Los Angeles County. When a work injury happens, California generally routes the claim through workers' compensation regardless of fault — but that's not always the end of the story. If a subcontractor, property owner, equipment manufacturer, or another driver contributed to the accident, a separate third-party injury claim may be possible alongside your comp benefits. Because many La Habra Heights residents work off-site or on properties owned by someone other than their employer, these third-party situations come up more often than people expect. LawProactive doesn't practice law — we simply connect injured workers with an independent attorney who can review the details and explain what paths may be open, without any upfront cost to you.

whyChoose.title: Why La Habra Heights Workers Reach Out to LawProactive

items.title: Comp Isn't Always the Whole Picture
items.desc: Workers' comp usually applies no matter who was at fault, but it doesn't rule out a separate claim against a negligent third party like a property owner or equipment maker.

items.title: You're Protected From Retaliation
items.desc: California law makes it illegal for an employer to punish you for reporting a workplace injury, and reporting within 30 days helps preserve your comp rights.

items.title: Deadlines Move Fast
items.desc: Third-party injury claims carry a two-year filing deadline, so getting matched with an attorney early gives more time to gather evidence and build the case.

items.question: I was hurt while driving for work near Harbor Boulevard or Hacienda Road — do I file workers' comp or a lawsuit?
items.answer: In most cases, you'd start with a workers' comp claim through your employer since it applies regardless of fault. But if another driver caused the crash, a separate third-party claim may also be possible. An independent attorney can look at the specifics and explain which paths apply to your situation.

items.question: What if my employer tells me not to report the injury?
items.answer: That's not something an employer can lawfully require. California protects your right to report a workplace injury, and retaliation for doing so is illegal. Reporting within 30 days also helps protect your ability to receive workers' comp benefits.

items.question: How long do I have to bring a third-party claim after a work injury?
items.answer: Third-party claims in California generally carry a two-year deadline from the date of the injury. This is separate from any workers' comp filing requirements, so it's worth having both reviewed by someone familiar with each track.
